stances.claim: Retired SC justices do not just stay home and sulk -- they change tires to embark on new journeys, with longer life spans than their predecessors a generation ago allowing them new careers in government (MCLE chair, Philja chancellor, JBC seat), international tribunals (ICJ, WTO, ILO), independent offices (Ombudsman, Comelec), UN ambassadorship, UP regency, and private-sector roles (law-school deanships, choosy law practice, corporate directorships).

Some retired SC members are choosy with their law practice -- Justice Feliciano (post-WTO) appears only in the SC and in Washington/Paris/Singapore international arbitration tribunals; CJ Puno with retired J. Mendoza serves as counsel for the Chamber of Mines in current SC litigation challenging the 1995 Mining Law's constitutionality.
Many retired justices become directors of private firms -- Puno (SMC, Union Bank), Davide (Manila Bulletin, Philippine Trust), and others on various corporate boards.

CJP's own post-retirement journey: Inquirer column writing (despite Salonga's discouragement that no retired chief justice has been a columnist -- CJP took it as agility-discipline for his mind and a platform to share humble views), independent directorships (where independence/integrity/probity/competence are required values familiar from the SC), declined regular teaching jobs and law-practice offers, but involved in Metrobank Foundation, Manila Cathedral Foundation, FLP (10 professorial chairs in 10 law schools), and Philippine Dispute Resolution Center.

notable_anecdotes: The 'reclusive life on Mount Olympus' framing -- CJP's recurring metaphor for the SC justices' insulated working life, used as the setup for the change-tires-not-stay-home thesis.

Salonga's discouraging quote -- 'No retired chief justice has become a columnist' -- and CJP's quiet decision to proceed anyway, taking the column as agility-discipline for his mind and a platform to share humble views. Among the most concrete anecdotes of CJP's post-retirement-Inquirer-column origin in the corpus.

Justice Feliciano's choosy practice -- appearing only in the SC and in Washington/Paris/Singapore international arbitration tribunals after his WTO Appellate Tribunal stint -- a model of dignified post-retirement practice.

CJ Puno + retired J. Vicente V. Mendoza serving as counsel for the Chamber of Mines in current SC litigation challenging the 1995 Mining Law's constitutionality -- a current-litigation detail flagged for readers.

The corporate-director roster -- Puno (SMC + Union Bank), Davide (Manila Bulletin + Philippine Trust), Bellosillo, Gutierrez (Purefoods + Ginebra), Melo (Fontana + Citystate), Nazario (San Miguel Properties + Ginebra), Ynares-Santiago (San Miguel Global Power), Vitug (Aboitiz Equity Ventures + ABS-CBN) -- among the most concentrated retired-justice-corporate-board listings in the corpus.
The four-track-private-sector taxonomy -- law-school deanship + return-to-law-practice + choosy-practice + corporate-director -- comprehensive coverage of retirement careers.

CJP's foundation portfolio -- Metrobank Foundation chair-of-advisers, Manila Cathedral Foundation president, FLP chair-of-trustees with 10 professorial chairs in 10 law schools, Philippine Dispute Resolution Center chair-emeritus -- among the most complete enumerations of CJP's post-retirement institutional roles.

The 'independence, integrity, probity and competence -- values I was used to in the Supreme Court' framing for independent-director work -- early CJP articulation of what later becomes the CIPI mnemonic in subsequent columns.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban answers reader questions about what Supreme Court justices do after retirement, given their reclusive life on Mount Olympus. Quoting the Constitution (justices hold office during good behavior until age 70 or incapacitation), he frames the answer: they just change tires for new journeys; life does not end at 70. Several government offices require retirement from the SC as a qualification -- MCLE chair (incumbent J. Bernardo P. Pardo), Philja chancellor (incumbent J. Adolfo S. Azcuna), and one of the four regular JBC members (vacant since July 2013). Some retired SC members go international -- CJ Cesar Bengzon (ICJ), J. Florentino P. Feliciano (WTO Appellate Tribunal), J. Flerida Ruth P. Romero (ILO). Others land in constitutionally independent offices -- J. Conchita Carpio Morales (Ombudsman; J. Conrado M. Vasquez was first Ombudsman), J. Jose A. R. Melo (Comelec, voluntarily retired after 2010). CJs Hilario G. Davide Jr. and Claudio Teehankee served as UN ambassadors; CJ Reynato S. Puno is a UP Board of Regents member. In the private sector, deanships of law schools -- Bellosillo (CEU), Chico-Nazario (UPHSD), Austria-Martinez (Adamson), Sandoval-Gutierrez (PLM). Some return to law practice -- J. Serafin Cuevas as Estrada and later Corona Senate-impeachment counsel; CJ Andres R. Narvasa as Estrada counsel. Some are choosy -- Feliciano appears only in the SC and in Washington/Paris/Singapore international arbitration tribunals; CJ Puno and retired J. Vicente V. Mendoza serve as counsel for the Chamber of Mines in current SC litigation challenging the 1995 Mining Law. Many become directors of private firms -- Puno (SMC, Union Bank), Davide (Manila Bulletin, Philippine Trust), Bellosillo, Gutierrez (Purefoods, Ginebra), Melo (Fontana, Citystate), Nazario (San Miguel Properties, Ginebra), Ynares-Santiago (San Miguel Global Power), Vitug (Aboitiz Equity Ventures, ABS-CBN). On his own post-retirement journey (after Dec 7 2006): Inquirer Chair Marixi R. Prieto invited him to write a column; former SP Jovito R. Salonga discouraged him with 'No retired chief justice has become a columnist,' but he proceeded -- column writing would force his mind to be agile and let him share humble views on public issues. He serves as independent member/adviser of boards of Philippine Stock Exchange-listed firms, helping them observe good-corporate-governance canons without representing management or any specific shareholder -- work that requires independence, integrity, probity, and competence, the same values he was used to in the SC. He prefers not to practice law (his old law firm dissolved when he joined the SC) and has declined regular teaching jobs and offers to rejoin government, but is involved in several foundations: chair of the board of advisers of Metrobank Foundation (which rewards excellence among teachers, soldiers, policemen, artists, journalists), president of the Manila Cathedral Foundation (overseeing the cathedral's reconstruction), chair of the board of trustees of the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity (which administers 10 professorial chairs in 10 law schools), and chair emeritus of the Philippine Dispute Resolution Center (promoting arbitration and mediation as alternatives to court litigation).
